paragraphs: The way the chief executive of the United States is to be chosen is almost the only important part of the system that has escaped harsh criticism, or has earned any word of approval from its opponents. The most plausible of them to appear in print has even condescended to admit that the election of the President is fairly well guarded.(1) I venture to go further, and I do not hesitate to say that if the method is not perfect, it is at least excellent. It combines, to an eminent degree, all the advantages that one could have wished to see combined.(E1)

It was desirable that the sense of the people should have a part in choosing the person to whom so important a trust would be given. This is achieved by giving the right of choice not to any body that already exists, but to men whom the people select for that special purpose and at that particular moment.

It was equally desirable that the immediate choice should be made by men best able to weigh the qualities suited to the office, and acting in circumstances that favor deliberation and a sound weighing of all the reasons and inducements that should govern their decision. A small number of persons, picked by their fellow citizens from the general mass, are the most likely to have the information and discernment that such complicated investigations require.

It was also especially desirable to give tumult and disorder as little opportunity as possible. This evil was not the least to be feared in choosing an official who would have so important a part in running the government as the President of the United States. But the precautions so happily devised in the system before us promise effective security against this harm. The choice of SEVERAL persons, forming an intermediate body of electors, is much less likely to throw the community into extraordinary or violent upheaval than the choice of ONE, who would himself be the final object of the public's wishes. And because the electors chosen in each State are to meet and vote in that State, their scattered and divided situation will expose them much less to the heats and ferments that could pass from them to the people than if they all had to be gathered at one time in one place.

Nothing was more to be desired than that every practicable obstacle be set against cabal, intrigue and corruption. These deadliest enemies of republican government might naturally be expected to approach from more than one direction, but chiefly from the desire of foreign powers to gain an improper influence in our councils. How could they better satisfy that desire than by raising one of their own creatures to the chief executive office of the Union? But the Convention has guarded against every danger of this kind with the most farsighted and judicious care. It has not made the appointment of the President depend on any bodies of men already in existence, who might be tampered with in advance and induced to sell their votes. It has instead referred the appointment in the first instance to a direct act of the people of America, to be used in choosing persons whose temporary and sole purpose is to make the appointment. And it has excluded from eligibility all those who, by their position, might be suspected of too much devotion to the President in office. No senator, representative or other person holding a place of trust or profit under the United States can be among the electors. In this way, without corrupting the body of the people, the immediate agents in the election will at least begin their task free of any sinister bias. Their short existence and their scattered situation, already noted, give good reason to expect that they will stay free of it to the end. Corruption on so large a scale, reaching so many men, takes time as well as money. Nor would it be easy to enlist them quickly, spread out as they would be over thirteen States, in any combination founded on motives that, though not properly called corrupt, might still mislead them from their duty.

Another desideratum, no less important, was that the Executive should depend for his continuance in office on no one but the people themselves. Otherwise he might be tempted to give up his duty out of eagerness to please those whose favor he needed to keep his official standing. This advantage too is secured, by making his re-election depend on a special body of representatives, appointed by the society for the single purpose of making this important choice.

All these advantages will happily come together in the plan devised by the Convention. The people of each State are to choose a number of electors equal to the number of senators and representatives that State has in the national government. These electors are to meet within the State and vote for some fit person as President. Their votes are then to be sent to the seat of the national government, and the person who happens to have a majority of the whole number of votes will be the President. But a majority might not always center on one man, and it might be unsafe to let anything less than a majority decide the matter. So it is provided that in such a case the House of Representatives shall choose, from the candidates with the five highest numbers of votes, the man who in their opinion is best qualified for the office.

The process of election gives a moral certainty that the office of President will never fall to anyone who does not possess, in an eminent degree, the necessary qualifications. Talents for low intrigue and the petty arts of popularity may be enough to lift a man to the first honors in a single State. It will take other talents, and a different kind of merit, to establish him in the esteem and confidence of the whole Union, or of so large a part of it as a successful candidate for the distinguished office of President of the United States would need. It will not be too strong to say that there will be a constant likelihood of seeing the office filled by characters of outstanding ability and virtue. Those who can appreciate how much the executive in any government shapes its good or bad administration will count this no small recommendation of the Constitution. We cannot accept the political heresy of the poet who says:

"For forms of government let fools contest—That which is best administered is best." Yet we may safely declare that the true test of a good government is its aptitude and tendency to produce a good administration.

The Vice-President is to be chosen in the same way as the President, with this difference: the Senate is to do, in the case of the Vice-President, what the House of Representatives is to do in the case of the President.

Some have objected that appointing a separate person as Vice-President is superfluous, if not harmful. They allege that it would have been better to authorize the Senate to elect an officer of that description from among its own members. But two considerations seem to justify the Convention's view. The first is that, to make certain the body can always reach a definite decision, its presiding officer must have only a casting vote. To take a State's senator out of his seat as senator and make him President of the Senate would be to trade, for the State he came from, a constant vote for a contingent one. The second is that the Vice-President may occasionally take the President's place in the supreme executive office, and so all the reasons that recommend the manner of election prescribed for the one apply with great, if not equal, force to the manner of appointing the other. It is remarkable that here, as in most other instances, the objection raised would lie equally against the constitution of this State. We have a Lieutenant-Governor, chosen by the people at large, who presides in the Senate and is the constitutional substitute for the Governor in emergencies like those that would authorize the Vice-President to exercise the authorities and discharge the duties of the President.
